$comment: The closed vocabulary of the ceramics domain. Each clay body, glaze and decoration gives its origin: the first year with a firm record, the place and, where known, the maker. circa = true marks an estimate. No origin means that no open source gives a year. A glaze lists the kinds of body that it suits.

branches.name: Tableware
branches.scope: Plates, bowls, cups, saucers and the full place setting: the ceramics of a meal.

branches.name: Tea and coffee ware
branches.scope: Teapots, tea bowls, caddies, jugs and coffee sets: the ceramics of a drink ritual.

branches.name: Kitchen and storage ware
branches.scope: Crocks, storage jars, ovenware, mixing bowls and pitchers: the work pots of a kitchen and a larder.

branches.name: Vases and display vessels
branches.scope: Vases, jars, chargers and bowls made to be looked at, and the studio vessel as a work of art.

branches.name: Figures and sculpture
branches.scope: Figurines, busts, animals, groups and ceramic sculpture.

branches.name: Tiles and wall ceramics
branches.scope: Wall and floor tiles, tile panels, mosaics and tiled stoves: ceramics as an interior surface.

branches.name: Architectural ceramics
branches.scope: Terracotta and faience cladding, roof tiles, ornamental brick and facade panels: ceramics on a building.

branches.name: Sanitary and technical ceramics
branches.scope: Basins, WCs, baths, electrical insulators and laboratory porcelain: fired clay as engineered product.

bodies.name: Earthenware
bodies.note: A porous body fired below about 1150 °C. Pots from Xianrendong Cave are the oldest known vessels of fired clay.

bodies.name: Terracotta
bodies.note: A red, iron-rich earthenware, often left unglazed. It makes figures, roof tiles and facade blocks.

bodies.name: Fired brick clay
bodies.note: A coarse clay fired in moulded blocks. Glazed brick makes the Ishtar Gate of Babylon, about 575 BC.

bodies.name: Egyptian faience
bodies.note: A body of ground quartz with an alkaline flux that glazes itself when it dries and fires. It is not a clay body.

bodies.name: Stonepaste (fritware)
bodies.note: A white body of ground quartz, glass frit and a little clay. Islamic potters used it to copy Chinese porcelain; Iznik ware uses it.

bodies.name: Stoneware
bodies.note: A dense, vitrified body fired at about 1200 to 1300 °C. It holds water without a glaze.

bodies.name: Red stoneware (zisha)
bodies.note: A fine iron-rich stoneware, left unglazed. Yixing teapots in this body take a patina from tea.

bodies.name: Porcelain
bodies.note: A white, dense and translucent body of kaolin and porcelain stone, fired at about 1300 °C.

bodies.name: European hard-paste porcelain

origin.by: Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus and Johann Friedrich Böttger

bodies.note: The first European true porcelain. The Meissen manufactory began production in 1710.

bodies.name: Soft-paste porcelain
bodies.note: A glassy body of white clay and frit, an early European imitation of Chinese porcelain. Sèvres used it until about 1770.

bodies.name: Bone china
bodies.note: A porcelain with calcined bone ash. It is white, thin and strong. Josiah Spode set the standard recipe about 1796.

bodies.name: Creamware
bodies.note: A cream-coloured earthenware with a lead glaze. Josiah Wedgwood refined it as Queen's ware in 1762.

bodies.name: Pearlware
bodies.note: Creamware with a little cobalt in the glaze, so that it looks whiter. It carries blue transfer prints well.

bodies.name: Jasperware
bodies.note: A fine unglazed stoneware coloured with metal oxides, with white relief in the same body.

bodies.name: Black basalt
bodies.note: A black unglazed stoneware coloured with iron and manganese, made for vases and teaware in the antique style.

bodies.name: Ironstone china
bodies.note: A hard, heavy, white body patented as a cheap substitute for porcelain.

bodies.name: Parian porcelain
bodies.note: An unglazed biscuit porcelain that looks like Parian marble. It made figures and busts for the Victorian home.

bodies.name: Raku clay
bodies.note: An open, grogged clay that survives the shock of a hot kiln. Pieces are hand-built, not thrown.

bodies.name: Vitreous china
bodies.note: A dense, white body with near zero water absorption, cast for sanitary ware: basins, WCs and urinals.

bodies.name: Fireclay
bodies.note: A refractory clay that resists heat and holds a large cast without warping: Belfast sinks, baths and kiln furniture.

bodies.name: Porcelain stoneware (gres porcellanato)
bodies.note: A pressed tile body with water absorption below 0.5 %. It makes floor and wall tiles that copy stone, wood and concrete.

bodies.name: Technical porcelain
bodies.note: A high-alumina porcelain for electrical insulators and laboratory ware. It resists voltage, heat and acids.

bodies.name: Paper clay
bodies.note: Clay mixed with paper fibre, so that thin sculptural forms stand and join when dry.

bodies.name: Glass-ceramic
bodies.note: A glass that heat turns into a fine crystal ceramic, so that it takes a flame and the freezer. Stookey found it by accident; Corning Ware used it from 1958.

bodies.name: Pyrogranite
bodies.note: A hard, frost-proof architectural body that the Zsolnay factory developed. It makes roof tiles, relief panels and finials with a strong glaze.

materials.name: Ormolu (gilt bronze)
materials.note: Fire-gilt bronze mounts that French dealers added to Chinese and Sèvres porcelain in the 18th century.

materials.name: Silver
materials.note: A metal for mounts, spouts and rims of precious ware.

materials.name: Brass
materials.note: A yellow alloy of copper and zinc for taps, fittings and frames.

materials.name: Chrome plate
materials.note: Bright chromium plate on brass or steel, the finish of taps and fittings after about 1925.

materials.name: Stainless steel
materials.note: A corrosion-resistant steel for lids, frames and modern fittings.

materials.name: Cane and bamboo
materials.note: Woven cane or bamboo for the overhead handles of teapots and kettles.

materials.name: Cork
materials.note: A bark used for the stoppers and lids of storage jars.

materials.name: Wood
materials.note: Timber for lids, stands, frames and toilet seats.

materials.name: Glass
materials.note: A non-ceramic glassy material. It is a substitute that breaks the look of fired clay.

materials.name: Plastic
materials.note: A moulded polymer, the usual substitute for ceramic in cheap ware.

materials.name: Concrete
materials.note: A cast stone that replaced terracotta and faience on facades after about 1930.

materials.name: Steel frame
materials.note: The structural frame behind terracotta and faience cladding.

glazes.name: Bare clay (unglazed)
glazes.note: No glaze: the fired clay is the surface. Bizen, Yixing, terracotta and jasper ware leave it bare.

glazes.name: Burnished
glazes.note: Clay polished with a stone or a bone before firing, so that it shines without a glaze.

glazes.name: Biscuit (unglazed porcelain)
glazes.note: Fired porcelain left without glaze, matte and white like marble. Vincennes and Sèvres used it for figures.

glazes.name: Attic black gloss
glazes.note: A fine iron-rich slip that turns black and glossy in a three-stage firing. It makes black- and red-figure ware.

glazes.name: Terra sigillata
glazes.note: A red gloss slip of very fine clay particles, the surface of Roman tableware.

glazes.name: Alkaline glaze
glazes.note: A glaze fluxed with soda or potash. It gives bright turquoise with copper and blue with cobalt.

glazes.name: Lead glaze

origin.place: China (Han dynasty) and the Roman world

glazes.note: A clear, low-fired glaze fluxed with lead oxide. It is glossy and takes colour from metal oxides.

glazes.name: Ash glaze
glazes.note: A glaze from wood ash. In a wood kiln it forms by itself as green-brown runs on the shoulder of a pot.

glazes.name: Celadon
glazes.note: A green to blue-green glaze from a little iron in reduction. Longquan and Korean Goryeo celadons are the classic forms.

glazes.name: Sancai (three-colour)
glazes.note: Lead glazes in amber, green and cream that run together on tomb figures and vessels.

glazes.name: Tin glaze
glazes.note: An opaque white lead glaze with tin oxide. It is the base of maiolica, faience and delftware.

glazes.name: Jun glaze
glazes.note: A thick opalescent blue glaze, often with purple splashes of copper.

glazes.name: Tenmoku
glazes.note: A dark iron glaze that breaks to brown on rims. Hare's fur and oil spot are its effects.

glazes.name: Crackle glaze

origin.place: China (Song dynasty, Guan and Ge wares)

glazes.note: A glaze that crazes in a net of lines on cooling. Potters stain the lines to show them.

glazes.name: Salt glaze
glazes.note: Salt thrown into a hot kiln forms a thin glaze with an orange-peel texture on stoneware.

glazes.name: Copper red
glazes.note: A red glaze from copper in reduction, hard to control: sang de boeuf and flambé.

glazes.name: Raku glaze
glazes.note: A low-fired glaze on a piece pulled hot from the kiln. Black and red raku tea bowls are the canonical forms.

glazes.name: Shino glaze
glazes.note: A thick white feldspar glaze with pinholes and fire-orange edges.

glazes.name: Oribe glaze
glazes.note: A copper-green glaze poured over part of a piece, named after the tea master Furuta Oribe.

glazes.name: Clear porcelain glaze
glazes.note: A transparent high-fired feldspar glaze that shows the white body and underglaze painting.

glazes.name: Victorian majolica glaze
glazes.note: Bright coloured lead glazes over moulded relief, shown at the Great Exhibition of 1851.

glazes.name: Crystalline glaze
glazes.note: A zinc glaze that grows flower-like crystals in a slow cool.

glazes.name: Matte glaze
glazes.note: A dry, velvet glaze. Grueby matte green set the surface of American art pottery.

glazes.name: Uranium oxide glaze

origin.by: Frederick Hurten Rhead for Homer Laughlin

glazes.note: A bright orange-red glaze coloured with uranium oxide, the red of Fiesta ware.

glazes.name: Lava glaze
glazes.note: A thick, bubbled glaze that looks like lava, the surface of West German Fat Lava vases.

glazes.name: Satin glaze
glazes.note: A glaze between matte and gloss, about 20 to 50 GU, common on studio and Scandinavian ware.

glazes.name: Sanitary glaze
glazes.note: A glossy, hard, white zircon glaze that cleans easily, sprayed on vitreous china and fireclay.

glazes.name: Coloured gloss glaze
glazes.note: A smooth, even, saturated industrial glaze in one colour.

glazes.name: Albany slip
glazes.note: A natural brown clay from Albany, New York, that melts to a dark glossy coat at stoneware heat. American potters dipped crocks and jugs in it.

glazes.name: Iron brown glaze
glazes.note: A glossy brown glaze coloured by iron oxide. It covers telegraph and power insulators, because it hides soot and dirt and sheds rain.

glazes.name: Eosin glaze
glazes.note: An iridescent lustre glaze in red, purple and gold that the Zsolnay factory made. It gives roof finials and wall panels an oily metallic sheen.

glazes.name: Soft-paste glaze
glazes.note: A soft, glassy lead glaze that fuses with the body of soft-paste porcelain. It pools in the corners and takes enamel colours well. English factories used it from about 1745.

decorations.name: Undecorated
decorations.note: No applied decoration: form, body and glaze alone make the piece.

decorations.name: Cord-impressed
decorations.note: Patterns pressed into wet clay with twisted cord, the mark that names Jōmon pottery.

decorations.name: Incised and carved
decorations.note: Lines cut or carved into the leather-hard clay, often under a glaze that pools in them.

decorations.name: Black-figure painting
decorations.note: Figures in black gloss slip on the red clay, with incised detail.

decorations.name: Red-figure painting
decorations.note: The ground is black gloss and the figures stay the red of the clay, drawn with a brush.

decorations.name: Lustre
decorations.note: A thin film of silver or copper fired in reduction on a glaze. It shines like metal.

decorations.name: Sgraffito
decorations.note: A line scratched through a slip to show the clay of another colour under it.

decorations.name: Iron-oxide painting
decorations.note: Brushwork in iron oxide that fires black or brown, under or over a glaze.

decorations.name: Slip inlay
decorations.note: Lines cut into the clay and filled with white and black slip, under a celadon glaze.

decorations.name: Encaustic inlay
decorations.note: A pattern of coloured clay inlaid into a tile, so that it does not wear off. Herbert Minton revived it in the 1830s.

decorations.name: Cut-tile mosaic
decorations.note: Glazed tiles cut into small shapes and set together in a geometric pattern.

decorations.name: Underglaze cobalt blue
decorations.note: Cobalt oxide painted on the raw body under a clear glaze: blue and white.

decorations.name: Cuerda seca
decorations.note: Coloured glazes held apart by a line of wax and manganese, so that they do not run together.

decorations.name: Overglaze enamel
decorations.note: Coloured glass enamels painted on a fired glaze and fixed in a low third firing.

decorations.name: Istoriato painting
decorations.note: Narrative scenes painted across the full surface of maiolica, after prints of paintings.

decorations.name: Underglaze polychrome
decorations.note: Several colours painted under a clear glaze, as on Iznik ware with its raised bole red.

decorations.name: Kintsugi
decorations.note: A repair of a broken piece with lacquer and gold dust, so that the break becomes a line of gold.

decorations.name: Slip trailing
decorations.note: Liquid slip trailed from a spout in lines and dots, as on English slipware.

decorations.name: Famille rose enamel
decorations.note: An opaque pink enamel of colloidal gold that adds soft shading to overglaze painting.

decorations.name: Agateware and marbling
decorations.note: Clays or slips of different colours mixed or combed, so that the pattern goes through the body.

decorations.name: Transfer printing
decorations.note: A pattern from an engraved copper plate printed on paper and moved to the ware. It made decoration cheap.

decorations.name: Mocha dendritic
decorations.note: A drop of acid colour on wet slip spreads into a pattern like a tree, on bands of turned ware.

decorations.name: Sprigged relief
decorations.note: Small relief motifs pressed in moulds and applied to the body, as on jasperware.

decorations.name: Moulded relief
decorations.note: Relief made in the mould with the piece itself.

decorations.name: Pierced and reticulated
decorations.note: Openwork cut through the wall of the piece.

decorations.name: Gilding
decorations.note: Gold fixed on the glaze in a low firing, then burnished or left bright.

decorations.name: Liquid bright gold
decorations.note: A gold resinate that fires bright without burnishing. It made gilding cheap.

decorations.name: Spongeware
decorations.note: Colour dabbed or stamped with a cut sponge, a cheap decoration for export ware.

decorations.name: Pâte-sur-pâte
decorations.note: Layers of white slip painted on a tinted body and carved, so that the relief looks translucent.

decorations.name: Hand banding
decorations.note: Lines of colour applied on a wheel at the rim and foot.

decorations.name: Decal
decorations.note: A printed transfer on a film that is slid onto the glaze and fired. It replaced hand transfer printing.

decorations.name: Screen print
decorations.note: A pattern printed through a mesh screen, used on tiles and tableware after about 1950.

decorations.name: Digital inkjet print
decorations.note: Ceramic inks printed by an inkjet head on tiles. It copies stone, wood and photographs.

decorations.name: Wax resist
decorations.note: Wax painted on the piece so that a glaze or slip does not take there.

decorations.name: Cold-painted pigment

origin.by: the workshops of the Qin imperial tomb

decorations.note: Lacquer and mineral pigments painted on a fired body and not fired again. The Qin terracotta soldiers carried it, and Tang tomb figures used it for faces.

decorations.name: Printed layer lines
decorations.note: The fine horizontal ridges that a clay printer leaves as it builds a wall in layers of 1 to 2 mm. Digital ceramics keep them as the surface.

decorations.name: Brushed white slip
decorations.note: White slip swept over a dark stoneware body with a coarse brush, so that the strokes show (hakeme in Japanese). Joseon buncheong potters made it a main decoration.

decorations.name: Stamped
decorations.note: Small dies pressed into the leather-hard clay in rows (inhwa), then filled with white slip. Buncheong potters of the early Joseon court used it on dishes and bottles.
